·
第2️⃣天：一整天深度玩转阿尔山秋景，早起看不动河的晨雾，河流边还有牛牛和漫山遍野的金黄橙红交织，午后光线柔和林间光影刚好，随手拍出森系治愈大片
·
第3️⃣天：阿尔山前往呼伦湖再到满洲里住宿，沿途是满目鎏金秋色，中午抵达呼伦湖，秋日湖面澄澈静谧小羊门悠闲踱步，傍晚抵达满洲里，逛异域风情街头，吃地道的内蒙火锅
·
第4️⃣ 天：从满洲里往呼伦湖解锁美丽的风车秋色，在呼伦湖荡秋千欣赏静谧的湖水，沿途前行抵达186彩带河，登高俯瞰蜿蜒曲折的额尔古纳河，傍晚抵达黑山头，赴一场草原绝美日落，晚餐吃当地特色的烧烤
·
第5️⃣天：从黑山头前往恩和俄式的童话乡村，彩色木刻楞小屋搭配秋日田园，满满的异域田园风情，午后打卡整片金黄白桦林秋风落叶氛围感拉满，一路游玩抵达额尔古纳休息，领队带我们去吃了牛排锅地道好吃
·
第6️⃣天：上午欣赏额尔古纳草原初秋的湿地黄绿渐变河道蜿蜒，成群的牛马过水美的不像话，下午奔赴莫日格勒河俯瞰天下第一曲水壮阔又温柔，在落日余晖下我们疯狂拍照记录下开心时刻，返回海拉尔吃了心心念念的俄餐
第7️⃣天：自由行简单逛逛，吃地道的内蒙火锅，然后返程
·

Day7：海拉尔→返程

items.text:
Published Oct 1, 2026, 5:31 AM EDT

Chris is a Senior News Writer for Collider. He can be found in an IMAX screen, with his eyes watering and his ears bleeding for his own pleasure. He joined the news team in 2022 and accidentally fell upwards into a senior position despite his best efforts.
For reasons unknown, he enjoys analyzing box office receipts, giant sharks, and has become known as the go-to man for all things Bosch, Mission: Impossible and Christopher Nolan in Collider's news division. Recently, he found himself yeehawing along to the Dutton saga on the Yellowstone Ranch.
He is proficient in sarcasm, wit, Photoshop and working unfeasibly long hours. Amongst his passions sit the likes of the history of the Walt Disney Company, the construction of theme parks, steam trains and binge-watching Gilmore Girls with a coffee that is just hot enough to scald him.
His obsession with the Apple TV+ series Silo is the subject of mockery within the Senior News channel, where his feelings about Taylor Sheridan's work are enough to make his fellow writers roll their eyes.

Silicon Valley has given us a lot of positive things, and a lot of, well, questionable people in its time. The home of technology and artificial intelligence, where Big Tech becomes so important to us that the world could collapse without it. Well, imagine if they also found away to commercialize time travel? Yes, it's not good. That's the setup behind the next huge sci-fi project that's somewhere between The Office and Back to the Future, with the filmmakers behind Project Hail Mary helping bring it to the big screen.

Universal Pictures is developing Paradox Inc., a feature adaptation of Forrest Brazeal's upcoming debut novel of the same name. Phil Lord and Christopher Miller will produce through Lord Miller, while Academy Award-winning filmmaker Daniel Roher (Navalny) is attached to direct.

The story revolves around the rivalry between a scrappy startup and a dysfunctional Big Tech corporation as both race to develop the world's first consumer time machine. The winner could potentially gain control over reality itself, although there's a fairly significant complication: Silicon Valley's version of time travel doesn't behave quite how anyone expects.

Brazeal knows the world he's skewering particularly well. The author previously worked at Google during the technology industry's AI and cryptocurrency booms, with his novel satirizing startup culture, hackers, corporate hubris and the industry's favorite philosophy of moving fast and breaking things. Time itself presumably wasn't supposed to be included in the “things” part.

Collider Exclusive · Sci-Fi Survival Quiz
Which Sci-Fi World Would You Survive?
The Matrix · Mad Max · Blade Runner · Dune · Star Wars

Five universes. Five completely different ways the future went wrong — or sideways, or up in flames. Only one of them is the world your instincts were built for. Eight questions will figure out which dystopia, galaxy, or desert wasteland you'd actually make it out of alive.

💊The Matrix

🔥Mad Max

🌧️Blade Runner

🏜️Dune

🚀Star Wars

TEST YOUR SURVIVAL →

01

You sense something is deeply wrong with the world around you. What do you do?
The first instinct is often the truest one.

APull on every thread until I understand the system — then figure out how to break it.
BStop asking questions and start stockpiling — food, fuel, weapons. Questions don't keep you alive.
CKeep my head down, observe carefully, and trust no one until I know who's pulling the strings.
DStudy the patterns. Every system has a rhythm — learn it, and you learn how to survive it.
EFind the people fighting back and join them. You can't fix a broken galaxy alone.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

In a world of scarcity, what resource do you guard most fiercely?
What we protect reveals what we believe survival actually requires.

AKnowledge. If you understand the system, you don't need resources — you can generate them.
BFuel. Everything else — movement, power, escape — runs on it.
CTrust. In a world of fakes and informants, a truly reliable ally is rarer than any commodity.
DWater. And after water, information — the two things empires are truly built on.
EShips and credits. The galaxy is big — you survive it by being able to move through it freely.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

What kind of threat keeps you up at night?
Fear is useful data — if you're honest about what you're actually afraid of.

AThat reality itself is a lie — that everything I experience has been constructed to keep me compliant.
BA raid. No warning, no mercy — just the roar of engines and then nothing left.
CBeing identified. Once someone with power decides you're a problem, you're already out of time.
DBeing outmanoeuvred — losing a political game I didn't even know I was playing.
EThe Empire tightening its grip until there's nowhere left to run.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

How do you deal with authority you don't trust?
Every dystopia has a power structure. Your approach to it determines everything.

ASubvert it from the inside — learn its rules well enough to weaponise them against it.
BIgnore it and stay out of its reach. The further from any power structure, the better.
CAppear to comply while doing exactly what I need to do. Visibility is the enemy.
DManoeuvre within it carefully. You can't beat a system you refuse to understand.
EResist openly when I have to. Some things are worth the risk of being seen.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

Which environment could you actually endure long-term?
Survival isn't just tactical — it's physical, psychological, and very much about where you are.

AUnderground bunkers and server rooms — cramped, artificial, but with access to everything that matters.
BOpen wasteland — brutal sun, no shelter, constant movement. At least the threat is honest.
CA dense, rain-soaked city where you can disappear into the crowd and nobody asks questions.
DMerciless desert — extreme heat, no water, and something enormous living beneath the sand.
EThe fringe — backwater planets and busy spaceports where the Empire's attention rarely reaches.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

Who do you want in your corner when things fall apart?
The company you keep is the clearest signal of who you actually are.

AA tight crew of believers who've seen behind the curtain and have nothing left to lose.
BOne or two people I'd trust with my life. Any more than that and someone talks.
CNobody, ideally. Alliances are liabilities. I work alone unless I have no choice.
DA community bound by shared hardship and mutual survival — people who need each other to last.
EA ragtag team with wildly different skills and total commitment when it counts.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

Where do you draw the line — if you draw one at all?
Every survivor eventually faces a moment that tests what they're actually made of.

AI won't harm the innocent — even the ones who'd report me without hesitation.
BI do what I have to to protect the people I've chosen. Everything else is negotiable.
CThe line shifts depending on who's asking and what's at stake.
DI draw a long-term line — nothing that compromises my people's future, even if it'd help now.
ESome lines, once crossed, can't be uncrossed. I know which ones they are.

NEXT QUESTION →

08

What would actually make survival worth it?
Staying alive is one thing. Having a reason to is another.

AWaking others up — dismantling the illusion so no one else has to live inside it.
BFinding somewhere — or someone — worth protecting. A reason to keep moving.
CAnswers. Understanding what I am, what any of this means, before time runs out.
DLegacy — shaping the future in a way that outlasts me by generations.
EFreedom — for myself, for others, for every world still living under someone else's boot.

REVEAL MY WORLD →

Your Fate Has Been Calculated
You'd Survive In…

Your answers point to the world your instincts were built for. This is the universe your temperament, your survival instincts, and your particular brand of stubbornness were made for.

The Resistance, Zion

The Matrix

You took the red pill a long time ago — probably before anyone offered it to you. You're a systems thinker who can't help but notice the seams in things.

You're drawn to understanding how the system works before figuring out how to break it.

You'd find the Resistance, or it would find you — your instinct for spotting constructed realities is the machines' worst nightmare.

You function best when you have access to information and the freedom to act on it.

The Matrix built an airtight prison. You'd be the one probing the walls for the door.

The Wasteland

Mad Max

The wasteland doesn't reward the clever or the well-connected — it rewards those who are hard to kill and harder to break. That's you.

You don't need comfort, community, or a cause larger than the next horizon.

You need a vehicle, a clear threat, and enough fuel to outrun it — and you're good at all three.

You are unsentimental enough to survive that world, and decent enough — just barely — to be something more than another raider.

In the wasteland, that distinction is everything.

Los Angeles, 2049

Blade Runner

You'd survive here because you know how to exist in moral grey areas without losing yourself completely.

You read people accurately, keep your circle small, and ask the questions others prefer not to answer.

In a city where humanity is a legal designation rather than a feeling, you hold onto something that keeps you functional.

You're not a hero. But you're not lost, either.

In Blade Runner's world, that distinction is everything.

Arrakis

Dune

Arrakis is the most hostile environment in the known universe — and you are precisely the kind of person it rewards.

Patience, discipline, and political awareness are your core strengths — and on Arrakis, they're survival tools.

You understand that the long game matters more than any single victory.

Others come to Dune and are consumed by it. You'd learn its logic and earn its respect.

In time, you wouldn't just survive Arrakis — you'd begin to reshape it.

A Galaxy Far, Far Away

Star Wars

The galaxy far, far away is vast, loud, and in a constant state of violent political upheaval — and you wouldn't have it any other way.

You find meaning in being part of something larger than yourself — a cause, a crew, a rebellion.

You'd gravitate toward the Rebellion, or the fringes, or whatever pocket of the galaxy still believes the Empire's grip can be broken.

You fight — not because you have to, but because standing aside isn't something you're capable of.

In Star Wars, that willingness is what makes all the difference.

↻ RETAKE THE QUIZ

Who Is Making Paradox Inc.?

Roher will direct and co-write a treatment with Matthew Robinson (Good Luck, Have Fun, Don't Die), who is adapting the screenplay. Lord and Miller produce alongside Lucy Kitada and Aditya Sood, while Brazeal serves as an executive producer. Universal Pictures and Lord Miller Productions are developing the feature.

Lord and Miller are the best names imaginable to be involved with a big, bold sci-fi comedy like this, because their work has constantly blended high-concept genre storytelling with comedy, including The LEGO Movie, Cloudy with a Chance of Meatballs, the Spider-Verse films and Project Hail Mary, so a workplace comedy about two warring companies who want to try and make more money than the other while taking advantage of our desire for nostalgia seems perfect.

The movie remains in development, with no production start or theatrical release date currently announced. Brazeal's novel, however, already has a date: Paradox Inc. will be published by Ballantine Books on January 27, 2027.

Release Date

March 15, 2026

Runtime

157 minutes

Director

Christopher Miller, Phil Lord

Based on the novel by Andy Weir (The Martian), Project Hail Mary is an action-adventure sci-fi film that stars Ryan Gosling as an astronaut who must save Earth from an oncoming ice age by heading to a faraway galaxy.

AUnderground bunkers and server rooms — cramped, artificial, but with access to everything that matters.
BOpen wasteland — brutal sun, no shelter, constant movement. At least the threat is honest.
CA dense, rain-soaked city where you can disappear into the crowd and nobody asks questions.
DMerciless desert — extreme heat, no water, and something enormous living beneath the sand.
EThe fringe — backwater planets and busy spaceports where the Empire's attention rarely reaches.
NEXT QUESTION →

Who do you want in your corner when things fall apart?
The company you keep is the clearest signal of who you actually are.

AA tight crew of believers who've seen behind the curtain and have nothing left to lose.
BOne or two people I'd trust with my life. Any more than that and someone talks.
CNobody, ideally. Alliances are liabilities. I work alone unless I have no choice.
DA community bound by shared hardship and mutual survival — people who need each other to last.
EA ragtag team with wildly different skills and total commitment when it counts.

Where do you draw the line — if you draw one at all?
Every survivor eventually faces a moment that tests what they're actually made of.

AI won't harm the innocent — even the ones who'd report me without hesitation.
BI do what I have to to protect the people I've chosen. Everything else is negotiable.
CThe line shifts depending on who's asking and what's at stake.
DI draw a long-term line — nothing that compromises my people's future, even if it'd help now.
ESome lines, once crossed, can't be uncrossed. I know which ones they are.
NEXT QUESTION →

What would actually make survival worth it?
Staying alive is one thing. Having a reason to is another.

AWaking others up — dismantling the illusion so no one else has to live inside it.
BFinding somewhere — or someone — worth protecting. A reason to keep moving.
CAnswers. Understanding what I am, what any of this means, before time runs out.
DLegacy — shaping the future in a way that outlasts me by generations.
EFreedom — for myself, for others, for every world still living under someone else's boot.

Your Fate Has Been Calculated
You'd Survive In…
Your answers point to the world your instincts were built for. This is the universe your temperament, your survival instincts, and your particular brand of stubbornness were made for.
The Resistance, Zion
The Matrix
You took the red pill a long time ago — probably before anyone offered it to you. You're a systems thinker who can't help but notice the seams in things.
You're drawn to understanding how the system works before figuring out how to break it.
You'd find the Resistance, or it would find you — your instinct for spotting constructed realities is the machines' worst nightmare.
You function best when you have access to information and the freedom to act on it.
The Matrix built an airtight prison. You'd be the one probing the walls for the door.
The Wasteland
Mad Max
The wasteland doesn't reward the clever or the well-connected — it rewards those who are hard to kill and harder to break. That's you.
You don't need comfort, community, or a cause larger than the next horizon.
You need a vehicle, a clear threat, and enough fuel to outrun it — and you're good at all three.
You are unsentimental enough to survive that world, and decent enough — just barely — to be something more than another raider.
In the wasteland, that distinction is everything.
Los Angeles, 2049
Blade Runner
You'd survive here because you know how to exist in moral grey areas without losing yourself completely.
You read people accurately, keep your circle small, and ask the questions others prefer not to answer.
In a city where humanity is a legal designation rather than a feeling, you hold onto something that keeps you functional.
You're not a hero. But you're not lost, either.
In Blade Runner's world, that distinction is everything.
Arrakis
Dune
Arrakis is the most hostile environment in the known universe — and you are precisely the kind of person it rewards.
Patience, discipline, and political awareness are your core strengths — and on Arrakis, they're survival tools.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/sharedimages/2024/11/direct-tv-logo.jpg?q=49&fit=contain&w=75&h=75&dpr=2
You understand that the long game matters more than any single victory.
Others come to Dune and are consumed by it. You'd learn its logic and earn its respect.
In time, you wouldn't just survive Arrakis — you'd begin to reshape it.
A Galaxy Far, Far Away
Star Wars
The galaxy far, far away is vast, loud, and in a constant state of violent political upheaval — and you wouldn't have it any other way.
You find meaning in being part of something larger than yourself — a cause, a crew, a rebellion.
You'd gravitate toward the Rebellion, or the fringes, or whatever pocket of the galaxy still believes the Empire's grip can be broken.
You fight — not because you have to, but because standing aside isn't something you're capable of.
In Star Wars, that willingness is what makes all the difference.

Lord and Miller produce alongside Lucy Kitada and Aditya Sood, while Brazeal serves as an executive producer. Universal Pictures and Lord Miller Productions are developing the feature.

Lord and Miller are the best names imaginable to be involved with a big, bold sci-fi comedy like this, because their work has constantly blended high-concept genre storytelling with comedy, including The LEGO Movie, Cloudy with a Chance of Meatballs, the Spider-Verse films and Project Hail Mary, so a workplace comedy about two warring companies who want to try and make more money than the other while taking advantage of our desire for nostalgia seems perfect.

items.title: Nvidia says my RTX 4070 Super isn't capable of Multi Frame Gen, but I'm surprised by how smooth this unofficial unlock actually feels
items.author: Jess Kinghorn
items.summary: Multi Frame Generation (or MFG) smoothes out gameplay by using AI to create as many as five generated, or 'fake' frames for each one actually rendered by the
items.text:
Multi Frame Generation (or MFG) smoothes out gameplay by using AI to create as many as five generated, or 'fake' frames for each one actually rendered by the GPU. Nvidia first introduced the original 2x Frame Generation feature with the RTX 40-series graphics cards back in 2022, but the highest rates of frame gen are reserved for the RTX 50-series.

If you have an RTX 5090 (despite it being particularly tricky to find one, let alone for a price anywhere near MSRP), you can enjoy as much as 6x MFG in supported games. This is because the RTX 50-series GPUs contain more powerful Tensor cores, but also a dedicated AI Management Processor (AMP) which works alongside Flip Metering to deliver frames, both rendered and AI-generated, to your display as smoothly as possible. Older cards, like my RTX 4070 Super, lack this snazzy silicon—but us PC gamers won't let something as silly as official limitations stop us.

I've already detailed how you can get 4x Multi Frame Generation working on an RTX 40-series GPU using some simple mods. I'll tell you what I found across all of my testing shortly, but first let me speedrun through how I got this working in the first place. Very simply, I used the ReShade HDR Installer to download unofficial mods that unlock higher rates of Multi Frame Generation for RTX 40-series cards. My RTX 4070 Super officially supports up to 2x MFG, but the unofficial mods mean I can test up to 6x MFG with this same card.

As Nvidia does not officially support more than 2x MFG on RTX 40-series cards, I was fully expecting some quirkiness ahead.

Even on an RTX 50-series card, officially supported Multi Frame Generation can introduce blurry frames and latency issues, so I'm not really expecting my RTX 4070 Super to fare better on those fronts. My testing is more about getting as much as I possibly can out of the hardware I already own, and silencing the voice that says I need to drop silly money on an RTX 50-series card at least for a little while longer.

Now, not all games support even the standard 2x MFG. So, let me tell you I was surprised to discover that story-heavy games like Lost Records: Bloom & Rage and The Thaumaturge both support up to 6x MFG (you can check Nvidia's full list of games that support MFG here). As such, the full roster of games I tested is a little non-traditional. It's worth noting too that I am only testing single-player games as the MFG unlock mods I'm using are not officially supported and can trigger in-game anti-cheat detection systems. Sorry, Arc Raiders, I don't want to get banned.

As for settings, I tested all games at 1440p resolution, and used High graphical settings. I also set the Nvidia DLSS quality mode to 'Balanced', and turned off ray tracing and similar tech where applicable. I set ReShade HDR Installer to tap out at 4x MFG as not all games support all the way up to 6x. My thinking was that more PC gamers might be interested in testing 4x MFG on an RTX 40-series card for that reason. I set no target frame rate beyond that, though, in the hopes that this experiment would give me the fullest picture of the highest highs and lowest lows in terms of frame rate.

Now, without further ado, let's take a look at some lovely bar charts.

blocks.x: Multi Frame Generation (or MFG) smoothes out gameplay by using AI to create as many as five generated, or 'fake' frames for each one actually rendered by the GPU. Nvidia first introduced the original 2x Frame Generation feature with the RTX 40-series graphics cards back in 2022, but the highest rates of frame gen are reserved for the RTX 50-series.

If you have an RTX 5090 (despite it being particularly tricky to find one, let alone for a price anywhere near MSRP), you can enjoy as much as 6x MFG in supported games. This is because the RTX 50-series GPUs contain more powerful Tensor cores, but also a dedicated AI Management Processor (AMP) which works alongside Flip Metering to deliver frames, both rendered and AI-generated, to your display as smoothly as possible. Older cards, like my RTX 4070 Super, lack this snazzy silicon—but us PC gamers won't let something as silly as official limitations stop us.

I've already detailed how you can get 4x Multi Frame Generation working on an RTX 40-series GPU using some simple mods. I'll tell you what I found across all of my testing shortly, but first let me speedrun through how I got this working in the first place. Very simply, I used the ReShade HDR Installer to download unofficial mods that unlock higher rates of Multi Frame Generation for RTX 40-series cards. My RTX 4070 Super officially supports up to 2x MFG, but the unofficial mods mean I can test up to 6x MFG with this same card.
As Nvidia does not officially support more than 2x MFG on RTX 40-series cards, I was fully expecting some quirkiness ahead.

Even on an RTX 50-series card, officially supported Multi Frame Generation can introduce blurry frames and latency issues, so I'm not really expecting my RTX 4070 Super to fare better on those fronts. My testing is more about getting as much as I possibly can out of the hardware I already own, and silencing the voice that says I need to drop silly money on an RTX 50-series card at least for a little while longer.

Now, not all games support even the standard 2x MFG. So, let me tell you I was surprised to discover that story-heavy games like Lost Records: Bloom & Rage and The Thaumaturge both support up to 6x MFG (you can check Nvidia's full list of games that support MFG here). As such, the full roster of games I tested is a little non-traditional. It's worth noting too that I am only testing single-player games as the MFG unlock mods I'm using are not officially supported and can trigger in-game anti-cheat detection systems. Sorry, Arc Raiders, I don't want to get banned.

As for settings, I tested all games at 1440p resolution, and used High graphical settings. I also set the Nvidia DLSS quality mode to 'Balanced', and turned off ray tracing and similar tech where applicable. I set ReShade HDR Installer to tap out at 4x MFG as not all games support all the way up to 6x. My thinking was that more PC gamers might be interested in testing 4x MFG on an RTX 40-series card for that reason. I set no target frame rate beyond that, though, in the hopes that this experiment would give me the fullest picture of the highest highs and lowest lows in terms of frame rate.

items.summary: The current gaming-themed season of Fortnite has been an opportunity for Epic Games to put assault rifles into the hands of a wide variety of iconic
items.text:
The current gaming-themed season of Fortnite has been an opportunity for Epic Games to put assault rifles into the hands of a wide variety of iconic characters. While his rival Shadow isn’t a stranger to packing heat, Sonic the Hedgehog typically sports a far more family-friendly persona than the one you can currently find running and gunning in the hit battle royale. Sega has been justifying this deviant behavior by arguing that the Sonic in Fortnite is not the real Sonic but an android Sonic. A new interview in Japanese magazine Famitsu sheds some light on how Epic convinced Sega to allow Sonic in the game in the first place, as well as revealing how some Japanese players have reacted to Sonic’s Fortnite debut.

In a joint interview between Sega president and COO Shuji Utsumi (who recently shared his desire to broaden the horizons of the company’s IP) and Takayuki Kawasaki, managing director of Epic Games Japan, the pair explained how a mutual respect between the companies and a particular love of Sonic from Epic Games President Tim Sweeney helped facilitate the collaboration. They also discussed how Sonic was retrofitted to work within the battle royale’s existing design templates, a process that required numerous iterations before a result could be agreed upon.

“We had a few problems with the proportions of his head to the rest of his body,” Utsumi said. “We also felt that the concept was great, but we had a lot of internal debate about whether it was right to just put Sonic into Fortnite as-is. We didn’t want it to feel like Sonic was included just because we received a request for such a collaboration, and we were conscious of the need to find alignment between the worlds of Sonic and Fortnite if he was to be included.”

He continued, “We didn’t want to let down Fortnite fans, but we also wanted to meet the expectations of Sonic fans too. It also wasn’t just about making his in-game appearance as strong as possible. There was a lot of work to do outside the game. We prepared our own backstory about why he exists in this world in this form, and crafted a story that was convincing and illustrated that as a comic.”

Revealing stats on player engagement with the collaboration, Kawasaki said it’s been a hit. “The response from players has been really positive,” he said, pointing out that Fortnite‘s overall player numbers were higher this season than in the same period a year earlier. “In just the first weekend following the launch, players worldwide collected over 1.5 billion rings and defeated Dr Eggman over 14 million times.”

With even Utsumi impressed by the numbers, Kawasaki added, “I guess, since they’re fighting a villain like Eggman, players don’t hold back when it comes to bullying him!”

The whole thing was a learning experience for Sega, Utsumi said. For Kawasaki, the current state of Fortnite, strengthened by its gaming-infused update, reinforces the promise of the metaverse as proselytized by CEO Tim Sweeney.

“Tim started talking about the metaverse more than 10 years before Fortnite even launched,” Kawasaki said. “One anecdote that left a strong impression on me was when he said, if kids are playing with action figures in a sandbox, none of them would say anything [like] ‘I have a Luke Skywalker figure, but you have Batman, and since he’s from DC, we can’t play together.’ But in the digital world, even before discussing legal rights, that’s already the norm. He wanted to change that. Everyone’s reaction at the time was that they understood, but it was basically impossible to implement. Then, before I knew it, Sonic was wearing a Mega Buster, and Goku was firing the kamehameha.”

“It really feels like the world Tim dreamed of is becoming a reality,” Utsumi said. “However, as this becomes more and more common, we [at Sega] have to work hard to establish our own worldview. items.text:
Yup, it's real. They did it.

Here's the full executive order, if you want to take it all in. Pity poor Sports Illustrated.

It's laughable, up there with similarly demented efforts to rename the Gulf of Mexico, Lake Ontario, and maybe New Mexico—I guess we'll see how that one ultimately shakes out. It's also pretty funny how "super intelligence" jibes with "Super Earth," the fascist homeworld of humanity in Helldivers 2. Probably just a coincidence, though.

Yet somehow, I'm not inclined to laugh. That the leader—ruler, really, at this point—of the most powerful nation on the planet can just whip out bizarre ideas like this and have them treated seriously is kind of frightening, isn't it?

And it is being taken seriously, at least insofar as we can describe billionaire tech oligarchs lining up to say and do pretty much whatever it takes to keep juicing the share price as seriousness: A subsequent White House Accord on Super Intelligence was signed by a who's-who of people who have made PC gaming almost impossibly expensive:

Sundar Pichai (Google)

Dario Amodei (Anthropic)

Mark Zuckerberg (Meta)

Greg Brockman (OpenAI)

Elon Musk (XAI)

Jensen Huang (Nvidia)

(Image credit: Getty Images - Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)And yes, they actually misspelled United States as "Unites States" under Trump's signature. Real pros at work here, top men all around.

Musk wasted no time publicly endorsing the rebranding on his X platform, although he was back to calling it AI less than eight hours later.

Super Intelligence https://t.co/ijlPkAmDBkSeptember 29, 2026

Huang also signalled his obedience, referring to "super intelligence" no fewer than three times in his own X post.

Yesterday at the White House, leaders from across our industry came together to sign the White House Accord on Super Intelligence.The principle is simple: the companies building this technology have the primary responsibility to develop and deploy it safely, and to be… pic.twitter.com/RGMDYs9bhsSeptember 30, 2026

Pichai, who was quick to acquiesce to Trump's demand to rename the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario for US users of Google Maps, heaped praise on the heads of the administration while also trotting out the phrase.

Great to meet today with @POTUS, @JDVance, @SpeakerJohnson and Administration + tech leaders. Important conversation and we signed today the White House Accord on Super Intelligence.As I shared today, Google has invested hundreds of billions in the last two years alone, with… pic.twitter.com/04EirBfyUXSeptember 30, 2026

And of course so did Zuckerberg, but on his own Facebook platform: "We believe superintelligence will create significant new opportunities for all people and businesses."

Humiliating prostrations notwithstanding, the practical impact of renaming artificial intelligence is basically nil: Apart from White House sycophants and quisling MAGA press outlets, nobody's calling it that.

But the bigger-picture consequences may be more, well, consequential: The accord, signed shortly after all the techbro billionaires lined up dutifully in a show of support for the latest addition to the president's world-changing "legacy," leaves the AI industry to regulate itself—"tremendous self-regulation," as Trump put it.

To quote from the accord: "In order to build a positive future for the American people and the world, we believe every company is responsible for developing its own technology safely and in a way that builds trust with customers and the public." It later states that "participating companies will meet regularly to establish standards and best practices to improve the safety of their systems." No mention of regulatory oversight, or any government involvement at all, is made.

Official. pic.twitter.com/BoTuIhxbTgSeptember 29, 2026

At least one big-name tech billionaire spoke out against the idea of self-regulation for the AI industry, although it bears remembering that he's not beholden to shareholders anymore.

"It’s fair to say that outside of the industry, the awareness of the dangers of A.I. is extremely low," Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates told the New York Times. "And you can say that of academia, you can say that of think tanks, you can say that of policymakers, politicians.

"And part of the reason I’m speaking so loudly—as loud as I can—is that you can’t rely on the industry to self-regulate here. I mean, it’s just insane."

So I guess, taking all that in, it's not really all that funny after all. But it sure is super.

items.author: Ethan Gach
items.summary: The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered has been out for over 24 hours now and there’s a small but loud contingent of players who aren’t sold on the game’s
items.text:
The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered has been out for over 24 hours now and there’s a small but loud contingent of players who aren’t sold on the game’s updated graphics. Tons of new visual detail sparkles underneath Improved ray tracing and overhauled lighting, but not everyone is on board with the brighter, less moody vibe the grim open-world RPG now sometimes evokes. As one player put it in a recent negative review on Steam, “the dark fantasy vibe is missing somewhere its like a Disney game.” Another post on the Steam Discussion page was less civil: “Dear CDPR remastered graphics look AWFUL.”

Those a growing split between these takes and those of returning players who are stunned by just how impressive the remaster look in some places. For every screenshot comparison showing greater visual fidelity at the expense of vibrancy, there’s one that shows The Witcher 3 looking better than it ever has. The whole debate is also muddied by the range of specs and platforms involved. New HDR effects might make the game look better on high-end displays but worse on screens that don’t support those effects. PC players with more powerful machines and deeper customization options might get a better result than players on a base PS5 where settings options are more limited.

You can start to get a very clear sense of the differences from a set of comparison screenshots shared by user itagouki on the Witcher subreddit (via Eurogamer). Things are much darker in the base version. There’s less detail. The contrast between light and shadow is starker. The remastered version is brighter, much crisper looking, and full of additional detail. But it definitely has a different vibe. Things are more evenly illuminated, and with bloom turned on, the game’s default setting, the visuals are bright to the point of appearing a bit washed out. Many players are blaming the path tracing, which appears to be sapping some of the boldness out of The Witcher 3‘s original aesthetic.

“I prefer the old look. It has better contrast, with stronger highlights and a more pronounced overall image,” itagouki wrote. “The Remastered color grading looks off to me. The contrast seems to have been flattened somewhat, and to compensate, the Remaster appears to use much stronger bloom, which brightens and softens the overall scene.” Other comparisons have shown a similar disparity. A clip of Geralt standing by the water in Novigrad looks flatter and more subdued in the Remastered version. “I was gonna say Remastered looks beautiful but then I realised it was on the left,” one fan wrote in response.

That’s something I’ve been experiencing a lot over the last day: seeing comparison shots and thinking the remaster looks pretty good, only to realize my eyes were drawn to footage from the base version. No doubt part of the issue is how snippets of captured gameplay and scenery ricocheting across social media, compressed and stripped out of the natural flow of the game, don’t do these comparisons any favors. There’s how the look of the game feels in a still image or brief clip, compared to how it feels when you’re actually playing it. So far, I definitely think some of the old art direction and magic is lost in the remastered version, but it’s not as obvious in the moment when I’m playing. And there are certainly places and moments in the new version, like foliage-filled fields in Skellige, that look truly impressive from the point of view of pure graphical fidelity, realism, and immersion.

“The game still looks good but for me it’s a straight downgrade from RT + max settings on Next Gen 4.04,” argued one player in a subreddit thread discussing the backlash to the game and general day-one negativity from some fans. “There seems to be some serious inconsistencies and issues with the lighting and tone mapper they opted for in the remaster.” Another player was much less forgiving. “[Nvidia] Hairworks is f*cked, RT/PT is f*cked, Bloom is f*cked….even the rasterized lighting (with RT turned off) has some f*ckery going on,” they wrote. “This is definitely NOT what I would expect from a so-called ‘remaster.’ Yes, there are some massive improvements to gameplay systems and shaders, but the lighting…wow.”

Time will tell if CD Projekt Red plans to take some additional passes to fine-tune the visual treatment in the remaster, or if it’ll leave players to fiddle with the options in their settings menus. At least on PC, anyone who is really ride-or-die for the original version can simply go into their Steam library and opt to download one of the previous iterations of the game instead of the latest overhaul.

items.title: I perished in the flesh pipes of Darktide's Depths of the Damned update, and you will too
items.author: James Archer
items.summary: Warhammer 40,000: Darktide continues to cling tightly, perhaps even aggressively, to my Steam installations, my occasionally waning interest repeatedly
items.text:
Warhammer 40,000: Darktide continues to cling tightly, perhaps even aggressively, to my Steam installations, my occasionally waning interest repeatedly re-sparked by the addition of akimbo-autopistolling chem fiends or haughty toasterpeople. A live service sucker, it makes me. Today's Depths of the Damned update, the grimdark co-op shooter's biggest since the Skitarii rocked up, continues the trend: it's centered around a massive new mission that's as revolting as it is compelling.

Whereas most Darktide excursions take you through criss-crossing sectors of its impossibly gigantic Hive City, the new Spillway deployment dumps you in the gushing, thus-unexplored hell of Tertium's water treatment facility. It’s a spectacular place, in the sense that it's utterly horrible. Fetid green liquid rushes through its caverns as blasphemous new life sprouts from the moisture, dark moss covering the cages that the complex's former gangster ownership probably didn’t hang for aesthetic reasons. The current residents aren't much friendlier, taking full advantage of the space's long sightlines to pelt you with lasgun fire while their fellow crusty cultists charge into melee range.

The Spillway's guts are even nastier. I'd say they’re covered in daemonic growths, but that would suggest the existence of visible points where the Chaos meat first took root. It would be more accurate to say the growths have become structurally integral to the facility in general, entire rooms covered floor-to-ceiling in the muck. The pipe network, meanwhile, is so thickly coated that it starts resembling a badly diseased intestinal tract; a playable Fantastic Voyage, if Raquel Welch was an Ogryn.

Despite this, and with the caveat that I've only played through the new mission once, it doesn't have the radically different feel of certain other post-launch operation additions. 2024's Rolling Steel was a runaway train caper unlike anything Darktide had tried before, and the Hive Scum update's No Man's Land op successfully swapped metal corridors for muddy trenches in a breathless WW1-inspired rush. Spillway is, at least structurally, a much more conventional oscillation of fierce wave combat and quieter traversal.

Those other two missions, however, were comparatively tight, short-form jaunts. This is a full-length, maybe even bumper-sized new challenge, which does at least try to enact some smaller twists along the way. There's a spot of light memory-puzzling, for example, as you’re shown a particular daub of gang graffiti that will mark the safe-ish path through the mazelike pipes – if you can find it among all the other gang graffiti. I don’t know if it’s a guaranteed spawn, but I was also ambushed partway through the upper facility by a traitor Captain, a foe usually reserved as the final boss for Assassination and Rolling Steel runs.

Spillway's actual final boss, which I’m slightly loathe to spoil (outside of the odd screenshot, naturally), almost manages to be a burst of freshness in a warren of filth. He's probably the most bosslike among all of Darktide's chunkiest baddies, advancing through phases, throwing out ruinous AoE attacks, and cackling through invulnerable periods like the mad space wizard he is. May your squads be smarter and more attentive than my gang of AI bots, or you’ll end up like me: a psychically flayed corpse, fallen without glory inside a lair made of poo chutes.

items.author: Clint Worthington

items.text:
It’s funny, looking back on 2026, that we’ll have gotten two televisual glimpses into the mind of the late, great chef and food writer Anthony Bourdain. One, Matt Johnson’s wry, tender biopic “Tony,” gives us a glimpse of the man’s larval form, the insecure, manipulative boy before he became the Tony we all knew and loved. The other? Bizarrely enough, an adaptation of a graphic novel he co-wrote in which a beleaguered chef with a checkered past punches, kicks, and decapitates his way (Casey Ryback-style) through a post-apocalyptic dystopia where haute cuisine carries enough cultural weight that people will kill for the right dish.

That’s the logline for “Get Jiro,” a graphic novel Bourdain penned in 2012 alongside Joel Rose, now adapted into a ten-episode Adult Swim series. The premise is so high-concept as to feel derivative, like a gumbo with too many disparate ingredients thrown together: In a resource-scarce future Los Angeles in which the populace entertains themselves with virtual reality, the only true sensory delights lie in food. Ergo, chefs have been elevated to a place of extreme cultural importance, mastering their craft like samurai and living like mob kingpins.

Living and cooking on the “Outer Ring” of this world is Jiro (Brian Tee), a stoic, unassuming sushi chef who, in the first episode, is approached by a sniveling dilettante at his humble locale to recruit him for greater things. But when the man insists on dipping his nigiri in soy sauce, Jiro’s blade gets another use besides slicing salmon, and the man’s head leaves his body. Unfortunately for Jiro, that becomes the first blow in a turf war that eventually sees him pitting two over-the-top rival chef kingpins, “Zatoichi”-style, against each other.

Get Jiro (Adult Swim)

All the components are there for a delightfully zany, bloody take on the yakuza/mob action thriller, with dishes as coveted as territory. But the original comic’s appeal lay in its vivid, grotesque artwork (by Langdon Foss) and the bona fides Bourdain’s name gave to its chef-flavored mayhem more than its story; Adult Swim’s adaptation loses the flavor of that artwork, dousing its well-worn cliches in unpalatable animation that feels more Flash animation than flashy.

Over the course of the first season’s ten episodes, Jiro is drawn further and further into the Inner Ring’s criminal underworld, battled over by Bob (Titus Welliver), a gruff, uncompromising maker of French international cuisine, and Rose (Allison Pill), a crunchy vegan who prides herself on ethical eating and no meat-is-murder dishes…though dispatching humans is a different story. Each wants Jiro’s talents with a blade (in any context) for their own reasons, and he’s more than happy to play them against each other, even as deeper scars from his family past begin to surface.

Granted, the show appeals most when it leans into the food-themed action: sniper-bakers who snuggle their rifle components in a series of baguettes, car chases evading variously themed food-truck bounty hunters, mob bosses drowning failed subordinates through what can only be described as “hollandaise-boarding.” The list goes on. Bourdain’s aim with the comic was clearly to send up the self-seriousness of chefs like himself, mixed with his love of samurai and yakuza movies, by building a fictional world where the tools and terms of chef culture become bloody weapons. Picture any “John Wick”-style action sequence set in a restaurant kitchen, and you get “Get Jiro”‘s whole deal.

Get Jiro (Adult Swim)

But after a few episodes, the novelty of the premise dissipates, and it gets harder to invest in the series’ twists and turns. As a character, Jiro remains pretty thin, his ronin-like stoicism buoyed mostly by the gradual reveal of his checkered past. His supporting cast offers little to offset that bitter taste; his allies consist of the well-meaning cop (Courtney Taylor) with her own relationship to food, and two innocent sisters (Seychelle Gabriel, Tessa Inez) whose proximity to Jiro put them in danger, most of whom don’t get enough to do to offset those formulaic roles.

The big later-show curveball comes in Justin Kirk‘s Alister, a Bourdain-like food critic whose relationship to Jiro’s cooking takes bizarre turns (especially after an episode featuring a violent escape from Butcher’s Block Prison, where all the big scary chefs get locked up). While the show mostly uses food as window dressing to add some seasoning to its been-there-done-that crime thriller action, Alister’s thread lets “Get Jiro” do what it does best: It actually explores our relationship to food and its various class signifiers.

It’s clear that shows like “Invincible” and “Blue Eye Samurai” have paved the way for something like “Get Jiro” to get made, and the animation style tries its level best to bring its over-the-top world to life. It’s clear showrunner Nate Cash (an old hand at “SpongeBob” and the director behind the brilliant “Over the Garden Wall”) had an uphill battle adapting this material for television, and it’s easy to relish the courses that feel pleasant on the tongue. If only the meal itself didn’t feel quite so bland.

All episodes screened for review. Premieres October 3rd on Adult Swim.

items.text:
Happy this week all! ...Ugh, you are all still here. When I went on holiday last week, I was hoping that I'd return to find that the whole "videogame journalism career" thing was just a fleeting delusion brought on by excess consumption of unripe pears. Perhaps I've actually been a wealthy gentleman gadabout this whole time, free of any need to keep the hellmouth topped up with layoff reports in order to stave off deprivation and disaster.

The one consolation - other than EIC Julian's many encouraging facial expressions and hand gestures – is that people are still making new PC games, and a few of them are actually quite interesting! Here's the latest list of new releases.

Monday 28th September

No, I refuse to believe that my holiday is over. Let's all get the heck down to Camp Whittlewood, a pixelart horror RPG about cub scouts going camping in the deep forest, featuring absolutely no serial killers.

Camp Whittlewood aside, there are precious few holiday-themed games on this list. Instead, we have games like HR: Human Remains. It's about being an office clerk in Hell, after humans lost a war with the demons. Get through your to-do list, or get fed to the Maw (no relation).

Yots is a PS1-ified co-op extraction game in which you repeatedly pillage a procgen city that looks like Silent Hill, assuming Silent Hill existed in the 1930s. I'm pretty sure it did. I don't think they had Pyramid Head technology back then, but they certainly had fog.

Speaking of lumbering metal monsters - where are my 90s Mechwarrior enjoyers? Drop Command is here with a mixture of cockpit combat and overarching 4X elements.

Tuesday 29th September

Nivalis Nights is a cyberpunk restaurant management game and life sim from the makers of Cloudpunk. The views should be pretty lush, whatever you may think of the jobbing element. Alas, my holiday!

Toem 2 is the new toem' up from John Toem, developer of Toem. (Actual studio name: Something We Made. Actual game description: a gentle diorama platformer and photography puzzler.)

Transport Fever 3 is the latest borderline masturbatory infrastructure meddler from Paradox, featuring the shiniest trains you ever did see.

From the makers of Human Fall Flat, here's Tiny Flock, a VR shepherding sim with more seesaws, circus machines and great white sharks than I believe is traditional, in real-life shepherding.

Wednesday 30th September

Radiosol casts you as a mechanical spider exploring a fallen world of attractively dusty and dessicated megastructures. It does use genAI to translate the game into Spanish, Japanese, German, French, and Chinese. I am underlining my own reminder to write/commission a piece on genAI translation in gamedev.

Okko The Exiled is a pretty gorgeous 2D sidescroller about some diminutive fellow with horns and a massive club. Look at him go!

Songs of Glimmerwick is a witch school RPG in which magic and music are closely allied. The developers are promising "hijinks". Don't… tempt me, Frodo!

Crusader Kings 3: By God Alone is the CK3 expansion in which you can run the Vatican and do all kinds of notionally un-Christian things – just ask Julian.

Thursday 1st October

Dynasty Warriors 3: Complete Edition Remastered is an Unreal Engineered revamp of the early noughties musou masher and its Xtreme Legends expandalone. Always had a sneaking fondness for DW games, despite the fact that they often play like lawnmower simulators in which the grass consists of shrieking spear guys.

RetroSpace (pictured) is the immersive sim with Saturday Night Fever vibes in which you, a janitor, try to survive inside a space station that has been yoinked into a blackhole.

There are planes in Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve, Bamco's latest Hot Shots-alike.

Friday 2nd October

What's the weather like there? On-going UK drought notwithstanding, we're edging into the golden season where you still get a few immaculate summer skies, but elegantly merged with the crispness and enchantment of autumn. Argh, having to undertake 'gainful employment' in these conditions is an offence to Nature. Now is the time to be out of doors, cavorting in the leaves, rather than staying inside to play/write about smelly videogames. Although if you have any new releases to recommend, we'd be interested as ever. Have a jolly week.

Gale of Waterdeep is rarely
items.text:
‘Baldur’s Gate 3’ Star Had No Idea About the Game’s Romance Until It Was Time to Record It [Exclusive]

Image via Larian Studios

Gale of Waterdeep is rarely at a loss for words. He can explain a complicated spell, talk through a crisis, and find time to charm the person standing next to him. The actor playing him, however, had no idea just how far that charm would go when he started recording Baldur’s Gate 3. Tim Downie recently revealed that he came into the project with very little information. It was his first video game role, and even after he was cast, he had to discover Gale’s personality through the scripts he received in the studio. The work went on for months before a routine Wednesday session introduced him to a part of the game everyone else apparently assumed he knew about.

Downie did not know players could romance Gale until he arrived to record the romance scenes. At a Baldur’s Gate 3 panel with narrator Amelia Tyler at FanX Salt Lake Comic Convention moderated by Collider's Maggie Lovitt, he recalled working on the game for about a year and a half without anyone mentioning its romances. “I think a lot of people just assumed I knew,” Downie said. When he asked what he was recording that day, the answer took him by surprise. Initially, he thought “romance scenes” meant flirting. Then he learned he would be performing the scenes in a motion capture suit without another actor opposite him. Downie described the revelation as a “baptism by fire,” and that first Wednesday turned out to be only the beginning.

Collider Exclusive · 8 Questions · 2 Minutes
Which Iconic Fandom Should You Join?
Harry Potter · Lord of the Rings · Star Wars · Star Trek

Eight honest questions about how you actually are: what you put on when you need cheering up, how deep you go into the things you love, what you argue about, what you keep on your shelf. Answer them and we will tell you where you belong. Four of the biggest fandoms on earth are taking new members, and they could not be more different from one another.

⚡Harry Potter(Wizarding World)

💍Lord of the Rings(Middle-earth)

⚔️Star Wars(A Galaxy Far Away)

🖖Star Trek(The Final Frontier)

FIND YOUR PEOPLE →

01

What do you put on when you need cheering up?
Nobody is brave about this one.

AThe same thing I have watched a hundred times.
BSomething long, slow and beautiful.
CSomething big and loud with a great score.
DOne clever episode of something hopeful.

02

How deep do you go into something you love?
There is no shallow end here, only different deep ends.

AI know every character and all the gossip.
BI have read the appendices and studied the maps.
CI have a ranked opinion on every instalment.
DI want to know how the world actually works.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

What do you and your friends actually argue about?
Every fandom has one argument it has been having for years.

AWhich one of us is which type.
BWhether the adaptation got it right.
CWhether the new stuff ruined the old stuff.
DWhether the right thing was actually done.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

How do you feel about a room full of strangers?
Every one of these comes with a very big room.

AGreat, and I will know everybody by the end.
BFine, as long as they take it seriously.
CBrilliant, especially if there is something to dress up for.
DHappy, provided the conversation is interesting.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

Where would you rather spend a week?
Pick on instinct rather than on budget.

AAn old castle somewhere rainy.
BMountains, long walks, no phone signal.
CA desert with an unbelievable night sky.
DA city built around a university.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

What do you believe about people, mostly?
All four of these stories have an answer, and they disagree.

AMost of them turn out better than expected.
BThe smallest ones decide the biggest things.
CAnybody can change, even very late on.
DWe work it out if we keep talking.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

What is actually on your shelf?
Look over at it before you answer.

AEverything I owned when I was twelve.
BHardbacks, in order, read more than once.
CFigures, posters, and a few things still boxed.
DBooks about how things work, plus a model or two.

NEXT QUESTION →

08

What do you actually want from a story?
Eight questions in, this is the one that picks your fandom.

BA world complete enough to get lost in.
CSomething huge I can share with everybody.
DAn idea that changes how I think.

Membership Confirmed
Your Fandom Is…

Four of the largest communities on the planet, and four completely
different reasons to belong to one. Here is yours, what it would give you, and the argument you
would be having within a week.

Wizarding World · Books 1997 · Films 2001

Harry Potter

You belong to the fandom that is really about comfort. Hogwarts
works on people because it is a place rather than a plot, and the pull is not the wizard war
so much as the corridors, the food, the weather and the sense that somebody is expecting
you.

You are drawn to belonging, which is why this fandom sorted itself into houses within
about five minutes and has never stopped.

This is the most social of the four, and the one most likely to know which type every
single person in your life would be.

The books are built to be reread rather than analysed, and rereading is exactly what you
do with things you love.

The new HBO series is bringing the whole thing back one book at a time, which means the
arguments are about to start all over again.

Middle-earth · Books 1954 · Films 2001

Lord of the Rings

You belong to the deepest fandom on this list, the one where
somebody has always read further than you and is quietly delighted to say so. Middle-earth
rewards patience more than any other world in popular culture.

You like the sense that the story you are reading is only the visible part of something
enormous, which is precisely how Tolkien built it.

This fandom takes adaptation seriously to a degree that other fandoms find slightly
alarming, and it has good reasons for that.

Your favourite thing about the books is probably the bit that is not action at all,
which is the walking, the songs and the long goodbyes.

Nobody here thinks heroism belongs to the powerful, and the whole story exists to make
that argument.

Star Wars

You belong to the loudest and largest tent of the four, the one
where three generations are all watching the same thing and none of them agree about any of
it. That disagreement is not a flaw in this fandom, it is the main activity.

You want something you can share with absolutely everybody, from a six year old to a

items.text:
Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Remake Release Date Update Is Good News

Published Oct 1, 2026, 5:24 AM EDT

James is a gaming writer from London who has spent thousands of hours exploring titles from every genre. Though he has a particular affinity for multiplayer titles like World of Warcraft, Destiny 2 and League of Legends, he has also put thousands of hours into single-player experiences, from deep RPGs to epic PC strategies. When he's not playing or writing, he can usually be found supporting his beloved Brentford FC.

The announcement of the Ocarina of Time Remake as part of The Legend of Zelda's 40th anniversary celebrations really did bring home just how significant a milestone it is for any gaming series. In what is sure to be a full circle moment for a lot of 90s gamers, we'll finally be able to revisit one of the best games of all time, only this time with modern visuals and gameplay features.

The initial confirmation really didn't give us any information about the game at all, but a dedicated Nintendo Direct has since answered many of the questions players may have had, including the specific date of its arrival. As we know, though, things are rarely smooth in the gaming industry, and there was every chance that the date would be moved to accommodate a little more development time.

Happily, the most recent update we have seen from the developer themselves should put those fears to bed, barring some kind of last-minute disaster.

Ocarina Of Time Is Still On Track For November

As first reported by Vice, Nintendo recently shared a detailed investor statement that goes into their financial state for the last year or so, as well as what their plans are moving forward. This included a detailed breakdown of upcoming sources of income, and several games were mentioned as part of that forecast:

"Nintendo Switch 2 is now in its second year since launch in June 2025 and sales continue to be strong. We aim to maintain the momentum for the hardware and see it delivered together with software into the hands of a wide range of consumers. The Nintendo Switch 2 software lineup added Splatoon Raiders in July, and titles scheduled for release include Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave in September, Nintendo Switch Sports Resort in October, and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time also in 2026."

That bodes well for Nintendo's current plans because we have already seen both Splatoon Raiders and Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave arrive bang on time, with Nintendo Switch Sports Resort up next this month. Unless something genuinely unprecedented happens, the currently scheduled release date of November 5 seems to be nailed on.

That gives it a couple of weeks of runway out in the wild before the arrival of GTA VI, with Ocarina remaining one of the few games that has been brave enough to launch in November at all.

Zelda Has Plenty More On The Way

Heading into 2027, Legend of Zelda fans also have the upcoming movie adaptation to look forward to. We now know a little more about what that is going to be like, with the film set to take place in a continuity all of its own, though many of the series' most familiar characters are still set to feature in some capacity.

Japan’s Smallest and Least-Populated Major Island Is a World of Pilgrimages, Delicious Food and Plenty of Forest Bathing

Each year, more than 100,000 people hike at least part of a 750-mile route on Shikoku that connects 88 Buddhist temples and other sacred sites

Laura Kiniry
| Travel Correspondent

September 29, 2026 3:40 p.m.

I had just arrived at Konsen-ji, the third temple on Japan’s Shikoku Pilgrimage route, when a young Japanese girl presented me with two origami cranes. These tiny gifts, I would later learn, symbolized wishes for a safe and smooth journey along the 750-mile circuit connecting 88 Buddhist temples, as well as other sacred sites, on Shikoku, the smallest and least populated of Japan’s four main islands.

On my week-long visit to Shikoku, I encountered many acts of kindness, from the innkeeper at Sudachi-an, a local guesthouse in the village of Nabeiwa, driving me to my lodging when I ended up lost in the rain, to a taxi driver insisting that I take a couple of sweet, kiyomi oranges to help sustain me on my day’s trek. This rural Japanese island is a place where history, hospitality and natural beauty converge.

The 7,063-square-mile island is the most rustic and remote. In fact, the first bridge connecting Shikoku to the main island of Honshu, where you’ll find big cities like Tokyo and Kyoto, wasn’t built until 1988. Even today, only three routes connect the two islands. Shikoku is a quiet rural slice of Japan where Westerners remain a rarity, though that’s slowly changing.

The Shikoku Pilgrimage is one of the island’s top draws for travelers. Between 100,000 and 150,000 people undertake at least part of the route annually, with the best times of year for walking the circular trail being spring and fall. All its sites are associated with Kobo Daishi, a Japanese monk who lived during the ninth century and founded Shingon, a major school of Buddhism that focuses on the attainment of enlightenment during a practitioner’s lifetime. While the individual temples and sacred sites span a variety of dates, mostly from the eighth century onward, the circuit itself wasn’t fully established until the late 16th to early 17th century. About 80 percent of the route is paved asphalt and concrete, often passing through small towns and farmlands. However, the rest of the pathway winds along dirt trails and ascends steep mountainsides and ancient stone steps through sections of remote wilderness. Along the way, pilgrims tend to stay in a mix of traditional ryokan (Japanese-style hotels), shukubo (temple stays) and local family inns. Most provide food, and some have onsens for bathing. While some Shikoku Henro (the Japanese word for “pilgrim”) set out to complete the entire 750 miles, many—like myself—choose to tackle only portions of it. Some people do it for spiritual reasons. Others are simply looking for a slower pace and to disconnect from the stressors of everyday life.

Armed with little more than the itinerary for my Oku Japan self-guided tour and a small day pack carrying my essentials (a local courier service makes it easy to ship larger luggage to stops along the way), I set out on a truncated five-day Shikoku Pilgrimage alone—determined to get off the grid. As it turns out, wandering among bamboo forests and towering cedar trees and along moss- and fern-laden trails taught me as much about the local culture as it did about myself. Arriving at each temple, I’d first clean my hands with a ladle at the outdoor hand-washing station and often drop a few coins into each main hall’s offering box, connecting it to a personal wish for things like good health and peace of mind. items.text:
The year might be drawing to a close, but it's a perfect time to do something new with your Japanese study! Take a look below at the latest list of Japanese learning resources, lovingly selected by our team, to help supercharge your Japanese study.

Activate Your Japanese!

Activate Your Japanese! is a 24-episode drama about a Vietnamese girl named Xuan who came to Japan to work in a hotel. It comes from Japan's national broadcasting network, known as NHK, which is known for producing quality video content about all sorts of topics. You can think of them as the BBC or CNN of Japan. In the drama, she encounters a sentient keychain, new friends, and lots of new Japanese. And as with any drama, there are elements of humor and romance that really make it entertaining.

Each video is divided into parts: The main skit, Today's Strategy, Onomatopoeia, and Welcome to My Japan. The main skit follows Xuan and her time adjusting to Japanese life, all while providing useful communication strategies. Next, the Today's Strategy section focuses on a useful communication strategy or phrase that Xuan utilized in the main skit. Plenty of examples are provided, making this part of each video particularly useful for learners. Then comes the Onomatopoeia bit, which introduces a common Japanese onomatopoeia. Again, several examples are provided to help reinforce how the word is used in real life. And finally, the Welcome to My Japan bit finishes off each video with a presentation of someone's life after coming to Japan. Many of these individuals immigrated to Japan for work and have lived in the country for several years. Their work, interests, and hobbies are highlighted in this section.

Every video in this series comes with translated captions and even a transcript, making it ideal for learners at level who want to practice reading or listening skills. But even if learning Japanese is not your main goal, the series can still be enjoyed purely as a drama for one's own entertainment. According to the site, this series will be available until 2027, so there's plenty of time to go through each of the 15-minute episodes.

Beyond Activate Your Japanese!, the NHK has a number of other resources for Japanese learners, like the Essential Japanese section, which provides survival phrases, and Easy Japanese: Conversation Lessons, which contains lots of learning content related to conversation practice. There's something for everyone, so check it out!

あかね的日本語教室

VIDEO

あかね的日本語教室, otherwise known as Akane's Japanese Class, is a popular YouTube channel produced by a Japanese teacher named Akane. This channel is targeted towards intermediate and advanced learners. However, Akane mentions that this channel is also accessible to beginners who want a bit of a challenge. The difficulty comes from all the videos being entirely in Japanese. The subtitles at the bottom of the screen are in Japanese, and include furigana over more difficult kanji. There are also closed captioning subtitles that can be turned off and on, with an impressive number of languages covered — 15!

The videos on this channel are very educational while also entertaining. The topics surround learning Japanese, travel around Japan, everyday life in Japan, and more. An example of Akane's videos that Japanese learners may find most useful are "[Business Japanese] Basics of telephone correspondence" and several interviews with non-native speakers living in Japan and studying the language. Each video lasts about 10-15 minutes in length, and they go by quickly. Because Akane speaks slowly, it's easy to follow the dialogue. If you're looking for even more content by Akane, you can also check out the podcast and Instagram page she also has.

Japanese Immersion with Asami

Japanese Immersion with Asami is a YouTube channel that, as the name suggests, focuses on teaching via comprehensible input; that is, Japanese made as easy to understand as possible, even for beginners, without relying on English explanations or translations. Asami has been a Japanese teacher since 2015, and with her trusty partner Hyougen, mostly reads stories in her videos, with helpful explanations and commentary; all in Japanese.

The videos are a great way to get your feet wet engaging with Japanese media more, without feeling like you're alone in the endeavor. In fact, the casual, supportive atmosphere of her videos might be their best feature; it really does feel like a private lesson. And with several series in a variety of genres and titles, such as Kiki's Delivery Service and short stories, you're sure to find a narrative that piques your interest.

日本語表現インフォ

One of the most difficult parts of learning another language can be expressions. As language conveys culture, each individual language has different expressions relevant to its own culture, and translating between them is no easy task. Thankfully for Japanese learners, there's the helpful website 日本語表現インフォ, or "Japanese Expression Info" to make things a little easier.

The site is very straightforward, with various expressions grouped into different categories, like expressions conveying emotions, sensations, or people, for example. From there they're often broken down even further, like expressions relevant to conveying different degrees of sadness.

While the website states the intent was to be a resource for people aiming to write in Japanese, it's helpful for Japanese learners as well. Not only will using these sorts of expressions add a sense of naturalness to your own writing, but they might help you while reading Japanese. 日本語表現インフォ is a great resource for learning both Japanese language and culture.

Sail

Sail is a unique approach to Japanese language exchange apps. Available on iOS and Android, Japanese learners first register for an account, filling out some of their interests and a basic self-introduction. But rather than connect with teachers or other language learners, Sail connects you to native Japanese speakers in the form of retirees and senior citizens. Like all similar apps, you're able to look at the profiles of various exchange partners, and find someone who might be a good fit in terms of interests and availability. Conversations are set to last 25 minutes, offering a contained experience: long enough that you're able to actually chat, but not so long that you might run out of steam.

It's a unique concept, and one that works well. Older people make good conversation partners, and are often very cordial and have a lot of free time. They're excited to get the chance to connect to learners, and share something of their language and culture, and this eagerness is contagious. What's even better is that Sail allows for unlimited conversations for a simple fee of $14.90 a month, with discounts at longer terms. This makes Sail one of the best bangs for your buck for Japanese learners hoping to converse.

パパパパパピィ

Update: Sadly this resource is no longer available.

Do you miss the good ol' days of reading picture books as a kid? Would you like to know more about Japanese children's books and the colorful images and themes they have inside? With the YouTube channel パパパパパピィ, you can read along, in a bedtime story fashion, to many different Japanese children's books.

Each story is read front to back by the host of the channel, who keeps you engaged with different voices and sounds, depending on the character or noise. You'll be able to follow along with the script, as the pages are shown while being narrated. Picture books are a great resource for beginner learners, as they don't have as many kanji. The readings are very short, witheach video being under ten minutes long. Whether you're looking to find more resources for your kids, or you're wanting to bring back the nostalgia of reading children's books, give this channel a go and watch how you're instantly transported to the land of cheery Japanese stories!

Megumi's Daily Japanese Adventures

If you're wanting to get more listening practice in, the podcast Megumi's Daily Japanese Adventures could be the right fit for you. This podcast was created for Japanese learners and could be used somewhat similarly to JLPT listening practice. In this podcast, the host, Megumi, talks about various experiences she's had related to travel, Japanese culture, and more. The way Megumi describes these adventures is story-like, with background music to accompany her anecdotes and detailed accounts. She speaks slowly and clearly, which is good for those who are just beginning to listen to content that's entirely in Japanese. The targeted audience for this podcast is around the intermediate level.

For listeners who would like to follow along with the dialogue, there are also transcripts on Megumi's website. At the end of these transcripts, there are English translations for some of the more advanced vocabulary. The episodes are around 5 minutes in length, so they're quick listens if you want to give them a go.

Human Japanese

Made by the same people who brought us Satori Reader, the Human Japanese apps are basically digital textbooks for Japanese, or as they call it, your "personal sensei in a box." There is an app for beginners and then an intermediate-level version. The beginner version boasts over 500 pages of content and around 800 example sentences, with breakdowns of each word and particle to boot! When teaching kana and kanji, there are stroke order animations, and plenty of example words as well.

The lessons in this app are truly worded and organized like a textbook. You will find lessons related to food, school, geography, health, work, and the weather. Major grammar points are included as well, including lessons on verbs, adjectives, adverbs, conjugations, counting, particles, and more. At the end of each lesson, you can find review quizzes. By default, you cannot move on to the next chapter until you have passed a chapter review quiz, but you can change this in the settings.

The overall design of the app is sleek and nice, but can feel a little dated to some seeing as it was originally created over a decade ago. Some pages are a little intimidating because of their word count, which some may find annoying. And there are no romaji to help you out; the app assumes you will learn hiragana and katakana. So if this kind of electronic textbook is just what you're looking for, then Human Japanese may be for you. For readers looking to give it a try, they offer a lite version free of charge.

YomuJP

For the Japanese graded reader junkies out there looking for more material, you might want to check out YomuJP. This website is dedicated to providing Japanese learners with easy, level-appropriate reading content in a simple layout.

There are tons of writings in their database. Each article contains pictures, and even audio recordings of a native speaker reading the material. This means you can use this site for listening practice as well. The stories are separated by reading difficulty. There are six categories, from N6 to N1, with N6 being the easiest (introductory level Japanese) and N1 being the hardest (advanced Japanese). According to the site, this scale is based on the Japanese Language Proficiency Test (JLPT) with N6 being an even easier level than the JLPT's lowest level of N5. You can browse articles by difficulty level or by tag.

The site also regularly posts to their Twitter page, often highlighting articles. New articles seem to be consistently released as well. If you are interested in practicing your reading (or listening) skills, or if you are thinking of studying for the JLPT, then consider YomuJP as one handy-dandy tool in your toolbox.

Thanks so much for following along with us to the end of the year, and the end of the article! We hope it's been a helpful journey. From all of us at Tofugu, hope you have a relaxing 正月, and spring is right around the corner.
